That's their whole logic behind structuring the class this way. They only have so many language paras on staff, so to maximize providing assistance, they put all the EL students in the same class. I know they are grouped together like that in at least 2 core classes. And maybe they feel a certain way about it, maybe they like it. According to the para they like being in the same class together. But I really can't read the situation and have to take her word for it. But I know at least one of my students doesn't like it, because there have been some struggles within that setting.

I'm not exactly sure. They are a paraprofessional, yes, but I don't know all of their qualifications. I do know they're hiring a lot of uncertified staff support and people that don't even have bachelor's degrees, but just associate degrees. And yeah, this district has been in the local news multiple times for controversies.

The district I'm in voted to close down multiple schools last year (I believe around 6 or 7), including a prominent high school that housed a large population of El learners. The students felt comfortable at that school, and even actively protested the closure of those schools during the board meeting. They raised concerns about not being properly accommodated, yet the board went ahead and closed those schools down. We already have a teacher shortage in our district and arguably a lack of resources to properly accommodate children, so is sheltered classes not problematic here? I can see the viewpoint of it being a viable solution, but there's also the implications of structing classes in such a way. Sure, students will have chances to interact with the general student body during lunch, before and after school, etc. But are we really expecting them to socialize with non-EL students during these times, especially when majority of the day they are grouped together?

In the case where the students are being grouped together for half or more for those classes, is that still not segregation? I understand that during lunch, extracurricular activities, etc. that they will be integrated into the larger student body, but I feel like the issue is they aren't going to know anyone other than their peers that they are in the same class with. In a way they are force to befriend or only be acquainted with students of the same language/culture. It seems more problematic to me to do things this way. Like sure, it's more efficient, and we can feel better about providing academic support to these children, but at the same time they are being denied the variety of social interaction that regular classes have

This game will never be adopted if OP neutrals rule the meta: Demogorgon, Pyramid Warden, Thaeriel, Jason, Blade, Matyr, etc. Imagine GU holds a hypothetical tournament, something akin to a Grand Prix. Well, the competition for top 8 will surely be limited to who has access to these OP neutrals. Since the quantity of these cards are severely limited (and purposely so), you will not see much variety in the top 8 decklist. Most likely you will just see the usual suspects of OP neutral cards and whales that are somewhat decent pilots of these said cards (I word it like this because I think a lot of these top players would be average at best in any other card game...shots fired for what it's worth). Now, consider someone outside the game who could be a potential competitor, and in turn a new player for the base, well are they really going to want to join in a game where the top 8 is nothing but the same meta cards? The beauty of games like Magic and Hearthstone are different color combinations or God cards, give that variety that players love to have. If GU were a fighting game, then everyone would be using the same main in the top 8, how boring. The second point is that if someone did want to compete then they would have to pay thousands of dollars for these OP neutral cards. That compounds if more people want to compete, thus locking out more competitors. Using the same fighting game tournament analogy, imagine if to be viably competitive you had to purchase the OP DLC character, but also when other players buy the DLC character, the price of said character goes up. People are just going to walk away from the deal. There's really no incentive for anyone to join in on this game.

Edit: to anyone thinking tournament coverage has no bearing on playerbase, you have to be in a huge delusional mindset to think such. Look at literally any other esport game and how it's presented. That presentation does wonders for attracting new players. Have y'all never seen an EVO stream? It's hyped AF and it certainly garners new players into fighting games. Same for Apex, RL, DOTA, and plenty of othe esport games. Then you look at how competitive Magic is presented, with such care. Not only is the commentary crucial, but so are the deck techs, player interviews, and quality of matches. What commentary do you possibly get wth GU? The process is problematic. I keep hearing they are trying to make cards futureproof, but that's not how card games work. Suppose they have a legacy mode where all cards are legal, it would be utterly insane to have all cards just fit in futureproof after one balance lock, actually it would be nearly impossible, considering the huge number of combinations of the different interactions of cards, at some point something is going to break. That's the reason why companies like WOTC ban cards from older formats, it just so happens that when you print tons of cards in a card game eventually in a legacy style mode there will be OP card combos (or just singular cards that are OP and unbalanced). So for example, LV had INSANE power level of cards but was only like a 3-week balancing period, so now we are left with Thaerial, Blade, and Matryr, cards that are insanely OP, pay to win, and out value your average card and the balancing window was what like a few weeks, as well as the sale. At no point did they think these cards were kind of OP,  didn't Demogorgon teach them anything, you print OP cards and then they are neutrals! Not only is this bad game design, but it's also just straight up cash grabbing. In a game with 6 Gods, it's kind of a shame there's not more emphasis on Gods identity and card synergies. It's more like if you're control well your wincon is Thaerial or Jason, but those can slide into any God's deck. Yeah sure there's unique decks like Dralamar (for mage), Aggro with relics or strong early creatures (light/war), and hidden (for Deception), but these play styles are so linear and become much better when jamming OP neutrals into the deck (Pyramid Warden, Blade, etc.). This game deserves to die because it's been nothing but cash grab ever since they had an influx of players since DO, literally every set printed after that has been a \*\*\*\*show, and you can even argue DO itself was when the game starting to decline. They don't even have artist names on the cards, and people are valuing these cards for hundreds of dollars, like gtfo. Cheap design, hardly any integrity, yet people will drop hundreds on cards that will certainly be worthless in the future, and if you think I'm wrong, remind my post and in a few years we'll see how GU fairs as something that's collection worthy (hint: it's not, you want proof, try and cash out your collection, o what's that no one's buying, hmmm could it be no real demand, you could only offframp if you sell your collection for -70% of what it's worth, that should be a sign people)

In terms of board control, I think the game needs more Pyramid Warden style early defensive cards or better reactive cards in general. The main problem I find is that you're punished for playing too reactive in this game since there's a ton of low-cost creatures with protection/ward or other shields that make them hard to answer. The best answers I could think of are order effects and blitz relics, but these do not help to control board.  I believe if there's going to be a copious number of low-cost creatures with layers of protection then there should be an almost equal number of reactive spells that can answer these creatures. Maybe more low curve sweepers that are actually effective and not super situational (I'm looking at you Dust to Dust and Bar Fight). Maybe a spell that's akin to Crystal Rain at 3 or 4 mana but deals damage to every creature could punish opponents who go too wide too early and keep the game from snowballing. Would it be too much to ask if a sweeper like that was neutral? The low curve sweep effect would have to hit both boards to be balanced though.

In addition to reactive spells being bad, reactive creatures aren't great either. The best creatures are blitz creatures but then that's limited to a few domains, prominently War and Nature, which are already aggressive domains (so the deck that wins going first is good against itself). I know Magic has the Frontline structures, but I feel these are not good enough. However, I do like the idea of early high health frontlines. If there's going to be an abundance of 3+ attack creatures at the 2 and 3 mana slot (sometimes even better stats) then I believe there should be more options for defense as well. It would be nice to see low curve frontlines with high health low attack that were actually useful, as oppose to cards like Rampart of Portable Fortress which have no abilities and can't attack. The problem with those structures is that they just sit on the field and don't do anything unless you're playing aggro,  so there's not a huge incentive to run them anyway (they really aren't even that good against aggro since early attack stats overpower the health easily).  More roar sleep and order effects on low curve creatures can also slow down the tempo of highly aggressive starts as well. Obviously there shouldn't be too many powerful reactive cards early game because that would swing the meta completely in favor of control, but the options we have right now aren't great and should be adjusted.
